# v2.70-dev — Training Tracker no longer runs as root

Until now the application process ran as **root** on both LXC and VM installs. It doesn't any more. A web app that handles logins has no business running as root, and this release fixes that.

**One command to finish the upgrade.** After updating to this release, run `sudo bash /opt/training-tracker/deploy/install.sh` once. The old updater predates all of this, so it cannot set up the service account while installing the release that introduces it. The script is safe to re-run, leaves your database and settings alone, and takes a few minutes. If you try the in-app updater first, it will tell you this rather than silently doing nothing. From here on, updates apply these changes themselves.

## What changed

**The app now runs as a dedicated unprivileged account.** The installer creates a `training-tracker` system user with no login shell, and the service runs under it inside a sandboxed systemd unit — no capabilities, a restricted syscall set, and a read-only view of the filesystem apart from its own directory.

**Updates still work, without granting the app any privilege.** The obvious way to let an unprivileged service restart itself is a `sudo` rule. We deliberately didn't do that. Every mechanism of that shape (sudoers, setuid helpers, polkit) hands the service an escalation capability, and every one of them depends on a package that may not be installed — minimal Debian LXC templates often ship without `sudo` entirely, so a sudoers-based design would break on exactly the platform this project targets.

Instead, the app **asks**. It writes a small request file it already owns; a root-owned systemd watcher notices, checks that the file really came from the service account and is the right size and shape, and then matches its contents against three fixed strings. Nothing else crosses the boundary — no filenames, no branch names, no arguments — so there is nothing there to tamper with. This needs no packages beyond systemd and util-linux, and behaves identically on an LXC and a VM.

**Less runs as root during an update, too.** Previously `npm install` ran as root during every update, which meant every package in the dependency tree could run install scripts with full privileges. Now the dependency install, database migration, build and database backup all run as the unprivileged account. Only the code fetch and the service restart still need root.

**The installer now fails loudly.** It checks everything it depends on up front and lists *all* missing pieces at once, instead of getting half way through and stopping — or, worse, appearing to succeed and failing later in production.

**Scheduled jobs are set up for you.** Automatic updates, report exports and the daily credential check are now installed as fixed system cron entries at install time, each running with the least privilege it needs. Changing the auto-update schedule in the app just updates the setting; the app no longer needs to edit the system's scheduled jobs to do it. A missed auto-update window (host asleep, for example) now runs late the same day rather than being skipped entirely.

## Fixed

- Saving a backup schedule silently did nothing if cron was unavailable or the account wasn't permitted to use it — it now tells you, instead of leaving you believing backups were scheduled when they weren't.
- The documented example for the credential-check cron job used an account that could never have read the configuration file, so it could not have worked as written.

## Notes

- Cron script logs have moved from `/var/log/training-tracker-*.log` into a single `/var/log/training-tracker/` directory.
- If you have changed `PORT` to a value below 1024, an unprivileged service cannot bind it. Either add `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` to `deploy/training-tracker.service`, or leave the port alone and put a reverse proxy in front — which is the better arrangement anyway.
